As of 217 PM EDT Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A slow moving upper level trough with associated closed 
surface low is beginning to enter the St. Lawrence Valley with the 
axis currently over eastern Ontario. Open wave showers and embedded 
thunderstorms within an area of 1000J/kg MUCAPE are tracking 
parallel to the St. Lawrence River, mainly west of the US-11 
corridor. This baroclinic zone will serve as the focal point for 
multiple rounds of showers throughout the day in the St. Lawrence 
Valley. Recent model guidance has continued the trend of keeping the 
heaviest of the convection and rain just across the International 
Border into Ontario. Nonetheless, given PWs to 1.8-2", and deep warm 
layer cloud depths, heavy rain is still possible in western St. 
Lawrence County where 1 to 1.5 inches of rain are expected through 
tonight. Locally up to 2 inches will be possible, especially under 
any convective elements in western St. Lawrence County. The WPC 
continues to highlight the St. Lawrence Valley with a Slight Risk 
(level 2 out of 4) for a 15% chance of exceeding flash flood 
guidance. While isolated urban flash flooding cannot be ruled out, 
significant enough rainfall capable of producing flooding is not 
anticipated over the prevailing flatter terrain. Outside of the 
North Country showers, channeled flow in the Champlain Valley will 
lead to intermittent gusts up to 25 mph near Lake Champlain. These 
gusts will taper down with the arrival of showers this evening.

The deformation boundary, and associated showers, will shift east 
into the Champlain Valley and Vermont this evening into tonight. A 
few spot light showers may be possible across Vermont this 
afternoon, but most will remain dry until later this evening. There 
is good agreement that overnight Sunday should have the better 
rainfall coverage and contain the bulk of the rainfall. A few areas 
of brief 0.25-0.5 inch/hour rates will be possible across northern 
New York within the boundary as it shifts east towards Vermont. 
Rainfall across Vermont is expected to range between half an inch 
and and an inch, with the higher amounts across the central and 
northern Greens.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A clearing cold front will sweep across the entire 
region from west to east, early to mid tomorrow morning, reaching 
Vermont by late tomorrow morning. Wrap around moisture along the 
convergent deformation band in northern New York will likely lead to 
some continued light shower chances (only 30-40%) through tomorrow 
afternoon. In Vermont, modest instability and shear could lead to an 
isolated strong thunderstorms in the late morning to early afternoon 
hours, primary east of VT-100. SBCAPE increases to 500-1500J/kg, 
with 30-40kts of shear would be sufficient for potentially an 
isolated strong thunderstorm. However, lingering low clouds from 
overnight rains, and competing updrafts along the front, may lead to 
lesser chances. The SPC does place most of eastern Vermont in a 
Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 5) for an isolated severe thunderstorm 
tomorrow afternoon. Expectations are that most storms if they 
develop would be sub-severe with plenty of cloud cover and 
stratiform rain around, but an isolated strong thunderstorm cannot 
be ruled out if an area can break out of the clouds and tap into 
some diurnal heating. Associated with the cold front, breezy, to 
locally gusty, winds are expected along the higher terrain and 
Champlain Valley tomorrow. As the front swings east, and associated 
strengthening 40-50 knot low level jet will move along the northern 
portions of the region. Gusts on summit levels could gust up to 30-
35 MPH, with valley winds around 20-30 MPH, mainly between 2 and 8 
PM. Winds will temper down with sunset and the development of a 
nocturnal inversion.

Showers and thunderstorms will taper off for most by late Monday 
afternoon. Lingering northwest wrap around flow could lead to some 
continued stubborn shower chances along the higher terrain of the 
northern Greens and Adirondacks Monday night. Across eastern 
Vermont, fog development appears likely in the valleys of the region 
with brief high pressure nudging in from the west, and calming 
winds. Tuesday and Wednesday will be quieter and calmer with 
temperatures in the upper 70s to mid 80s and mostly clear skies. 
Dewpoints will slowly creep up by mid week however, approaching the 
mid 60s in some places.

KEY MESSAGE 3: No significant changes to the forecast for later this 
week/next weekend, as we look to remain squeezed between a strong 
Bermuda high to our east and troughiness across the Northern/Central 
Plains. This will place us square under broad W/SW flow, with upper 
shortwaves occasionally rippling overhead. Humidity will increase as 
moisture streams northward into our region; dewpoints look to
